newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD-Australian markets focus on CPI.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD-Australian markets focus on CPI.

text.p: Australian financial markets will quickly get back into the swing of things after the Australia Day holiday with the release of CPI data at home on Wednesday and GDP and employment cost data due from the U.S.
The data are expected to add support for those arguing for monetary policy changes in both economies.
But the argument in Australia is over whether to cut rates while debate in the U.S. centres on whether rates should rise.

The local inflation data is expected to show that the moderation of inflation through 1996 continued in the fourth quarter and economists say the outlook is for further moderation through the first half of 1997. Average and median forecasts see CPI up 0.3 percent in the quarter and 1.6 percent year on year.
Underlying inflation is seen up 0.4 percent in the quarter and 2.1 percent year on year (for full consensus forecasts type AU/ECI and hit f9 key).
But markets will not be looking for an immediate rate cut, even if the inflation outlook remains.
Economists said that any move would most likely follow the release of November quarter wages data due next week. And then there is the ACTU's 'living wage' claim.

"While the inflation outlook looks stunningly good, a potential hurdle for the RBA is the ACTU's living wage claim," said Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson. "Any further rate cuts will probably have to wait until the outcome of the case, due late February at the earliest," he said.

The markets will also be assessing a speech by RBA deputy governor Stephen Grenville on Friday for policy clues. The government may also provide some grist for the mill this week if it releases its mid-year budget review, due any time now.

Friday will also mark the last release of monthly current account data. From next month, there will be a quarterly current account report and a monthly balance of trade and services report if Bureau of Statistics recomendations are adopted.
The December deficit is expected to stay under the A$2.0 billion level, despite a rise in imports, as exports are expected to rebound strongly after some recent weakness.

The current account has been, through the years, one of the most watched pieces of economic data, mainly when it was rising. A sharp rise in the deficit in 1986 led to then Treasurer Paul Keating's famous "banana republic" quote. Former Reserve Bank Governor Bernie Fraser said last year that national stress levels would be lowered dramatically if less attention was paid to the monthly deficit figures.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Fri: 10-yr cash 7.38 pct, 3-yr 6.62 pct)

Bonds will be waiting, as they were all of last week, for Wednesday's inflation data. The expectation of a set of bond-friendly data has been underpinning the market in recent weeks but traders have been unable to ignore a weakening U.S. market which is concerned about the prospect of rising rates.
But while Australian bonds may be buoyed by the possibility of a local easing, they will also be weighed on by the possibilty of a near term lift in U.S. rates.
The outlook for U.S. rates will be heavily influenced by employment cost index data due on Tuesday and GDP data on Friday.

"The Employment Cost Index is the most significant feature," said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "It's the most important price statistic since the Crusades."
According to a Reuters poll, economists, on average, are forecasting a 0.9 percent rise in the fourth-quarter ECI and a strong, 3.9 percent expansion in fourth-quarter GDP.

Markets remain concerned after recent warnings from the Federal Reserve that signs of potential wage pressures may elicit a response in the form of higher rates, as would signs of of strong growth in the GDP data.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri: US$0.7731/36)
The dollar looks set to probe lower again near term after heavy offshore selling saw it breach support at US$0.7740 last week to end the week 1/2 cent down.

The currency had found bids from local corporates and some Asian investors at 77 cents, but the technical momentum was strongly bearish and most analysts looked for an eventual test of the US$0.7680 low from August last year.
If this key chart bulwark were to break, then a long term downtrend to 75 or even 73 cents was on the cards, they said.
However, much would depend on what the consumer price data on Wednesday had to say about the prospects for another easing in domestic monetary policy.
Three cuts last year and the risk of another had narrowed the local dollar's yield advantage over its U.S. counterpart to levels where offshore investors had begun to shift funds the latter's way.
A low inflation reading would be seen as a green light for another cut and have the dollar testing SU$0.7680 in no time.
Equally, a higher than expected number would cool speculation and could well trigger a short covering rally back to 78 cents, dealers said.
The local currency should remain well supported against the yen and mark given that the sluggish Japanese and German economies meant rates there would be staying at record lows for months to come.

"With ... domestic data expected to do little to hurt easing speculation, the AUD will probably flounder around the US0.77 mark, leaning on the USD for support on the crosses," Commonwealth Bank economists said in a weely report.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS (Fri: All Ords 2423.0, -11.50)
With local corporate events thin on the ground, the market focus in a holiday-shortened week switches back to a shaky-looking Wall Street.
Continued weakness there would almost certainly transmit locally with many investors still disbelieving of Wall Street's recent record run.
"It's all Wall Street," said Andrew Sekely, head of equities at Intersuisse. "If Wall Street is not performing then why would you expect other markets around the world to do so?"
Economic data of interest will be December quarter inflation figures on Wednesday and what this means for interest rates.
Major companies reporting half year results this week include MIM Holdings Ltd and North Ltd, both reporting on Friday.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
